ABI: Application binary interface: the machine-level agreement for calling a function across a compiled boundary.
actor: An identity used to decide which operations are authorized; a domain actor is distinct from a background task.
allocation: Reserving a region of memory through an allocator. Its physical placement is not determined solely by a Rust type name.
AST: Abstract syntax tree: structured data representing the meaning and nesting of parsed syntax.
async: Code that returns a future whose execution can suspend while waiting, allowing other work to progress.
atomic: An operation observed indivisibly for the relevant memory location or transaction contract; the word needs its scope stated.
authentication: Establishing an identity. It is separate from deciding what that identity may do.
authorization: Checking whether the current identity may perform a particular action on a particular resource.
backpressure: A way for a bounded consumer to slow or reject producers rather than accumulate unlimited work.
borrow: Temporary access to a value owned elsewhere, checked against rules for aliasing, mutation and validity.
cancellation: A request to stop work; the contract must state when it is observed, what is rolled back, and what can already have happened.
capacity: An explicit upper resource limit, such as queued items, active tasks or initialized array slots.
checksum: A computed value used to detect some accidental corruption; an ordinary checksum is not a cryptographic authenticity proof.
closure: A callable value that can capture values from its surrounding scope, with ownership appropriate to its use.
coherence: Rules ensuring that trait implementation selection is consistent across crates.
compaction: Rewriting persistent state into a smaller equivalent representation while preserving a declared recovery contract.
consensus: Agreement among participants under a specified failure model; a demonstration of replication is not automatically consensus.
crate: A Rust compilation unit, either a library or an executable. A Cargo package may contain several targets.
deadline: The latest permitted completion time for a whole operation or specified phase; distinguish it from repeated per-attempt timeouts.
deadlock: A cycle or blocked dependency in which participants cannot make progress, even if memory accesses are safe.
deduplication: Recognizing a repeated operation by stable identity so that the intended effect is not applied twice within the stated scope.
DOM: Document Object Model: the browser object tree representing a document and its interactive elements.
drop: The end of an owned value’s lifetime, when its destructor releases resources according to its type’s contract.
durability: A persistence promise across specified failures. Writing, flushing and synchronizing provide different evidence.
edition: A selected set of Rust language compatibility rules for one crate, separate from the compiler release.
enum: A type whose value is one of a defined set of variants, optionally carrying associated data.
FFI: Foreign function interface: calling or exposing functions across language boundaries with explicit ABI and safety contracts.
framing: Defining where messages begin and end in a byte stream such as TCP.
future: A value representing asynchronous work that advances when polled and may report Pending before completing.
generic: Code parameterized by a type, lifetime or const value so one implementation can express several concrete cases.
heap: A conceptual name for allocator-managed storage; optimizer behavior and actual placement require separate reasoning.
hydration: Attaching client-side interactive behavior to HTML produced by server rendering.
idempotency: A contract under which repeating an identified operation has the same intended effect as applying it once.
invariant: A property that must remain true across every accepted state transition.
isolation: Rules controlling how concurrent transactions observe and affect one another.
iterator: A stateful producer of a sequence of values, commonly advanced lazily by a consumer.
lease: Time-bounded permission to act, whose expiry, clock assumptions and fencing rules must be specified.
lifetime: A relationship describing how long a reference remains valid; annotations do not keep dead owners alive.
linearization: Choosing a conceptual instant when an operation takes effect for a specified concurrent history.
lockfile: A record of resolved dependency versions used to reproduce a build; it does not guarantee absence of vulnerabilities.
mise: The course’s tool-version manager; mise.toml pins Rust and mise exec selects it for commands.
monomorphization: Compiler generation of concrete code for generic type instantiations, with possible code-size and optimization effects.
move: Transfer of ownership, after which the source binding cannot be used as the former owner unless the type is Copy.
MSRV: Minimum supported Rust version: a compatibility claim that requires its own testing scope.
mutex: A synchronization primitive allowing one holder at a time to access protected state.
newtype: A local wrapper type that gives an existing representation a distinct domain meaning and API boundary.
no_std: A crate mode using core instead of the full standard library; it does not by itself provide a firmware runtime.
ownership: Rust’s model for responsibility over values, their access and resource release.
panic: Abnormal control flow for violated assumptions or unrecoverable situations; ordinary input failures generally belong in Result.
pinning: A contract preventing certain values from being moved through a pointer, needed by some address-sensitive state.
polling: Asking an operation to make progress; browser periodic polling and Rust Future::poll are different mechanisms.
RAII: Resource acquisition is initialization: owned values acquire resources and release them in Drop.
replay: Re-applying recorded events in a defined order to reconstruct or study state.
schema: A contract describing data shape and constraints, whether for a database, a file or an API.
semaphore: A resource counter limiting the number of concurrent holders; a permit represents one share of that budget.
slice: A borrowed view of contiguous elements, carrying a pointer and length under its validity contract.
SLO: Service-level objective: a measurable target for a defined user-visible behavior over a stated window.
stack: A conceptual model for call-local storage and frames, not a guarantee that every local Rust value occupies a physical stack slot.
struct: A type grouping named fields under one representation and API.
TCP: An ordered reliable byte-stream transport between endpoints; it does not preserve application message boundaries.
TLS: A protocol providing authenticated encrypted transport under its certificate and endpoint trust assumptions.
trait: A named interface or set of capabilities that a type can implement.
transaction: A grouped state operation with declared atomicity and isolation semantics; it is not automatically serializable.
UTF-8: A variable-length encoding of Unicode scalar values. Byte offsets are not interchangeable with character positions.
WASM: WebAssembly: a portable executable format used here inside the browser’s capability and event-loop model.
zero-copy: A claim that specified data copies are avoided across a named boundary; it does not mean zero allocation or zero work.
